anchors.paper_title: An Implantable Device that Converses with Patients and Learns to Co-Manage Epilepsy
anchors.reason: The dataset README names this medRxiv paper (Goldblum, Shi et al.) as its paper. It reports the same 13-patient scalp and SEEG EMU recordings and shares authors with the dataset.
Candidate is a Pennsieve record for a single subject (PennEPI00037) from the same lab, not the 13-patient Human-AI co-management dataset; likely a separate data source.

metadata.methods_description: Patients underwent continuous video-EEG monitoring in the Penn Level 4 epilepsy monitoring unit, with scalp EEG sampled at 256 Hz and SEEG at 1024 Hz. Seizure detection used bandpass filtering (0.5-100 Hz scalp, 0.5-250 Hz iEEG), 60 and 120 Hz notch filtering, and common average or bipolar re-referencing. Annotations from clinicians and from patients via the smartphone platform were converted to BIDS events files.

citation_details.abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures that are not controlled by medication; and implantable devices are an exciting option for treatment. These devices improve seizure control and can detect impending attacks, missed medication, and impaired cognition. Unfortunately, they have no way to share this information with their hosts in real-time - a limitation common to most medical devices. This is a missed opportunity for implants and wearables to learn from patients, focus on what matters most to them, and teach them how their behavior affects their health. Here, we present a device platform that converses with patients and learns to co-manage epilepsy. citation_details.title: Artificial Intelligence as the Computational Framework for Adaptive Closed-Loop Neuromodulation in Psychiatry
citation_details.author: Babak Mahmoudi
citation_details.abstract: Adaptive neuromodulation offers a path toward personalized neuropsychiatric treatment by allowing therapy to respond to clinically meaningful neurophysiological and behavioral changes. Its clearest clinical precedents are responsive neurostimulation for epilepsy and adaptive deep brain stimulation for movement disorders. Both rely on signals that can be measured reliably and linked directly to stimulation. Psychiatric disorders pose a different problem: symptoms are heterogeneous, evolve over multiple timescales, and are observed only indirectly through noisy and incomplete measurements. Artificial intelligence can provide data-driven components of an adaptive neuromodulation system, connecting multimodal sensing, inference of patient state, prediction of treatment response, and constrained therapeutic adaptation. citation_details.title: Position: Agents Orchestrate, Policy Enforces — A Deterministic Tool-Use Control Pattern for Agentic Assistants over Sensitive EEG Data
citation_details.author: Sofio Katamadze, Ankur Chattopadhyay
citation_details.abstract: Agents that use language models to call external tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are entering sensitive environments, such as assistants that take action based on the emotional state they infer using electroencephalography (EEG). Prompt injection, tool poisoning, and unauthorized tool invocation threaten such agents while they act on state derived from identity-bearing EEG data. The position of this paper is that tool-use security cannot rely on the model’s decision, because the channel that carries legitimate instructions also carries the attack. The agent should issue action requests, but leave authorization to a deterministic policy engine. Three trust boundaries with ordered controls, mapped to an MCP threat taxonomy, implement the approach. citation_details.abstract: Abstract Importance Implantable sub-scalp EEG systems with a small number of channels have emerged as promising solutions for long-term seizure monitoring in patients with epilepsy. How seizure detection performance varies by montage configuration is unknown. Objective To quantify how automated seizure detection performance differs between full and reduced montages, and how these differences vary by epilepsy characteristics. Participants EEG data from 2281 consecutive EMU admissions between January 2017 and December 2024 were screened. Admissions with at least one annotated seizure and one interictal clip ≥20 minutes from any seizure were included. citation_details.title: Detecting and Improving Human Cognitive State in Real-Time Using Data-Driven Adaptive Systems: A Systematic Review
citation_details.author: Abhineet Rajendra Kulkarni, Pranav Madhav Kuber
citation_details.abstract: Changes in human attention, workload, or alertness over time can affect task performance and may even increase the risk of injury. Detecting these changes in real time can be beneficial in improving system performance and safety. We reviewed 27 studies that developed models to sense physiological signals, classify one's cognitive state, and deliver automated intervention. Interventions included providing real-time feedback, adjusting the task's difficulty, or modifying automation levels across driving, education, rehabilitation, and human-robot collaboration applications. The findings showed that electroencephalography (EEG) sensors were used in 70% of studies, with attention (56%) and mental workload (26%) considered as the most targeted cognitive states. Within-subject classification reached 81.85-95.81% for multi-class tasks in laboratory settings.
